lf_tollgate.name: Longford — the toll rail
lf_tollgate.desc: A barred rail spans the ford-road, iron-strapped and new enough to shine. Crown tents stand behind it in neat rows, and Captain Voss waits at the rail, already naming a toll before you've said a word.
lf_tollgate.brief: The toll rail, and Captain Voss waiting.

in.lockedMsg: Voss and his rail stand between you and the road beyond.
in.hint: force, bargain, or expose the captain's toll first

variants.brief: The rail, broken open. Voss is gone.
variants.desc: The rail hangs open on a bent hinge, and Voss is gone from his own camp — off wherever a captain goes once the rail he held stops holding anything.

variants.brief: The rail stands. A fixed toll, kept.
variants.desc: The rail still bars the road, but Voss keeps to the fixed sum now, posted plain beside it, and doesn't pad the figure when he names it.

variants.brief: The rail, open, under a Watch guard.
variants.desc: The rail stands open under a Watch guard, and Voss stands with it, waiting on an escort to Highward to answer for a writ he never read aloud.

actions.label: weigh what this toll is really asking
fx: Break the rail and it's down for good, but Voss remembers who broke it. Buy him off and the toll lives on, fairer. Prove him a liar and it's his own Crown that ends it.

actions.label: break the rail apart (might)
fx: The iron strap gives before the hinge does, and then both go. Voss doesn't reach for a blade — he reaches for someone still willing to stop you, and doesn't find one.
The rail holds, iron-strapped tighter than it looks. Voss watches you fail to break it with something close to satisfaction.

actions.label: buy him a standing cut (gold)
fx: Voss weighs the coin, names a fixed sum for the board, and has it lettered before you're back across. Not free. Not what it was, either.

lf_far_bank.name: Longford — the far bank
lf_far_bank.desc: The road opens out past the rail, wagon-ruts worn deep by traffic that never used to have to ask permission. Whatever Voss's toll paid for, this stretch of road looks no different for it.
lf_far_bank.brief: The road, past the rail at last.

variants.brief: The far road, quiet, the camp abandoned.
variants.desc: The road opens out past the rail. Voss's tents stand half-struck, abandoned in a hurry, and nobody has come to finish breaking camp.

variants.brief: The far road, the camp packing to leave.
variants.desc: The road opens out past the rail. Voss's men strike camp under a Watch officer's eye, in no rush and in no position to argue about the pace.

actions.label: search the tent-line
fx: A camp strongbox, unlocked, forgotten in whatever order sent everyone moving. Four coin left in it, and a ledger nobody will miss now.

lf_keeping_grant.name: the keeping-fee grant
lf_keeping_grant.hint: a sealed Crown grant, genuine, naming the ford a free crossing kept at the Crown's own expense

lf_voss.name: Captain Voss
lf_voss.desc: Crown-commissioned, or was, and wears the rail behind him like it proves the difference.
onDeath: Voss goes down at his own rail, and the toll dies with him. Nobody left at the tent-line moves to collect it after.

topics.label: what's the toll
topics.say: Everyone crossing at Longford pays the captain's toll. Coin's simplest. I've had worse offered, and taken it.

topics.label: whether he has the right to it
topics.say: "I've a Crown seal and a rail, and that's writ enough for anyone standing where you're standing." He says it fast, the way a man does when the actual words of the actual grant aren't the ones he wants read aloud.

topics.label: talk the toll down (will)
topics.say: Go on, then. Make your case.
fx: You talk him down from a toll he can't defend to one he can. "Fixed sum," he says, like it was his idea. "Posted plain. No more doubling it."
He hears you out and doesn't move a figure. "Fair's a word," he says. "Coin's a number."

topics.label: confront him with the grant (wits)
topics.say: You lay the keeping-grant flat on the rail-post, where his own toll-board stands.
fx: He reads it twice, the color going out of his argument along with his face, and doesn't reach for the rail again.
He reads it, hands it back, and says it proves nothing a stranger's owed an answer for. He's wrong about the paper, and knows it.

topics.label: confront him, Nye backing (wits)
topics.say: You lay the keeping-grant flat on the rail-post, and Corporal Nye steps up beside you to read it too.
fx: Voss reads it once, sees Nye already writing, and doesn't waste breath arguing with two witnesses and a Crown seal at once.
He reads it, hands it back, and says it proves nothing — with Nye standing right there watching him say it.

topics.label: press him on his own writ (wits)
topics.say: You say back to him, word for word, the keeping-fee terms he let slip and didn't mean to.
fx: He can't unsay his own writ back to himself. Something in his face gives out before the rest of him agrees to it.
"Words," he says. "Yours against a Crown seal." He's not wrong yet, and you don't have enough to make him wrong.

topics.label: press his writ, Nye backing (wits)
topics.say: You say back to him, word for word, the keeping-fee terms he let slip — with Corporal Nye there to hear it too.
fx: He can't unsay his own writ back to himself, not with the Watch already writing it down.
"Words," he says. "Yours against a Crown seal." Nye's pen stops. Not yet, it says.

topics.label: step back from the rail
topics.say: He doesn't watch you go. He's already naming a toll to whoever's next.

stages.text: Voss answers for his own writ now. The ford stands free, and everyone crossing it knows why.
The toll's fixed now, posted plain — not free, but fair, and Voss keeps to it.
The rail's down. Voss doesn't hold this crossing anymore.
You have proof enough to call the captain's toll a lie to his face — or force the rail, or buy him off.
A Crown captain charges what the road will bear at Longford. Force him, buy him off, or prove his toll's a lie.
You have proof enough that Voss's toll was never his to charge. Take it to him.
Nan's grandmother kept a keeping-fee grant once, under the ferry-house floor — if Voss's men never found it.
Marren doubts the true terms of Voss's toll are on his public board. Ask Nan, or press the captain on it himself.
Marren says the toll's doubled twice since she first crossed. Press her on whether he had any right to raise it.
Something about the captain's toll doesn't square with a fair one. Marren at Rowan's Cross might know why.
Nye wrote it up plain, whatever happened at the rail. An honest report, for once — he could get used to it.
Nye will carry real proof to Highward himself, or stand behind you while you do. Bring him to the rail.
Nye suspects the captain's stretched his writ, but a feeling doesn't move anyone. He'd need proof.
Corporal Nye keeps the road at Longford, and keeps his own counsel about the captain across the water.
Aldric's gone on, three days of grace left and a clear road under him. He'll make the rite window.
Aldric is carrying his sister's ashes to the Broken Oar Chapel, and the toll is eating what little grace he has left.
An old man waits at Rowan's Cross with a shrine-token worn smooth by thumbing.
Nan says it plain: the years don't come back, but the next thirty go to somebody. That'll do, she says.
Nan ran this crossing free thirty years before Voss's rail. She's still waiting on the water to need her again.
Eda mentions a ferrywoman put out of work by the captain's toll. She might talk, at the old ferry house.

epilogue.text: The rail at Longford came down by force, and stayed down. Voss doesn't hold the crossing anymore.
Longford's toll is fixed now, posted plain, and Voss keeps to the number he agreed to.
Voss answered for his own writ at Longford, and the ford runs free both ways again.
The rail still stands at Longford, and Voss still names what he pleases to cross it.
Aldric made the rite window with three days to spare, his sister's ashes carried to the Broken Oar Chapel at last.
Nan didn't get thirty years back. She got the next thirty handed to somebody else, and called that enough.
Someone found the old dry-season shallows above Longford, the crossing Voss's rail never thought to watch.
